title: International Trade and Balance of Payments

blocks.text: Nigeria sells crude oil and cocoa and buys wheat, medicines and refined petrol. That two-way flow is not charity and it is not an accident of geography alone. Trade pays when each country specialises in what it is relatively better at — even if one country is better at everything — and then settles the difference in foreign exchange through the balance of payments.

blocks.title: Absolute and comparative advantage
blocks.text: **Absolute advantage** (Adam Smith) means a country can produce more of a good with the same resources than another country. **Comparative advantage** (David Ricardo) means a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost. Comparative advantage is the basis of mutually beneficial trade even when one country has an absolute advantage in both goods.

headers: Opportunity cost of 1 bag of cocoa
blocks.caption: The partner has an absolute advantage in both goods, yet Nigeria has the comparative advantage in cocoa

blocks.title: Reading comparative advantage from opportunity cost
blocks.prompt: Using the table above, show which country should specialise in cocoa and which in cloth, and explain why both can still gain from trade.

steps.text: Absolute advantage: the partner produces more cocoa (10 > 8) and more cloth (20 > 4) per worker, so it is more efficient at both.
Nigeria's opportunity cost of one extra bag of cocoa is 4/8 = 0.5 bolt of cloth. The partner's cost is 20/10 = 2 bolts.
Cloth: Nigeria gives up 8/4 = 2 bags of cocoa per bolt; the partner gives up only 10/20 = 0.5 bag. The partner has the lower opportunity cost of cloth.
Therefore Nigeria specialises in cocoa and the partner in cloth. A trading price between 0.5 and 2 bolts per bag of cocoa leaves both better off than producing both goods at home.
The lesson: look at opportunity cost, not at who is 'better' in absolute terms. That is the question WAEC and JAMB actually set.

blocks.answer: Nigeria specialises in cocoa; the partner specialises in cloth; both gain if they trade at a rate between 0.5 and 2 bolts per bag

blocks.markdown:
### Balance of trade and balance of payments

The **balance of trade** is visible (merchandise) exports minus visible imports — oil, cocoa, machinery. A trade surplus means visible exports exceed visible imports.

The **balance of payments (BOP)** is the systematic record of **all** economic transactions between residents and the rest of the world in a period. It has two main accounts at this level:

- **Current account** — goods (the trade balance), services (shipping, banking, travel), income (interest, dividends, workers' remittances treated as current transfers or primary income, depending on the presentation) and current transfers.
- **Capital and financial account** — capital transfers, direct investment, portfolio investment (NGX-related flows), loans and changes in reserve assets.

In an accounting sense the BOP always balances: a current-account deficit is financed by a capital inflow or by running down foreign reserves. Examiners who ask you to 'correct a BOP deficit' mean an overall or current-account deficit that is draining reserves.

items: **Tariff** — a tax on imports, which raises the domestic price and protects local producers.
**Quota** — a physical limit on the quantity that may be imported.
**Embargo** — a complete ban on trade with a country or in a commodity.
**Exchange control** — official rationing of foreign currency, so importers cannot buy as much as they wish.
**Export subsidy** — a payment that makes local goods cheaper abroad.

**Devaluation / depreciation** — a fall in the naira's external value, which cheapens exports and dearens imports, helping to close a deficit if demand is elastic enough (Marshall–Lerner condition at a higher level).
**Expenditure-reducing policy** — tighter fiscal and monetary policy, so residents import less.

blocks.markdown: Protection is defended as a way to infant industries, to save foreign exchange, to protect jobs and to raise revenue. The costs are dearer goods for consumers, inefficiency behind the tariff wall, retaliation, and a smaller market for Nigeria's own exports. After the 1986 Structural Adjustment Programme Nigeria moved, unevenly, from heavy quantitative controls towards more tariff-based and market-based adjustment — including naira depreciation — as the preferred way to treat a payments deficit.

blocks.title: Balance of trade is not the whole of the balance of payments
blocks.text: A country can have a trade surplus on crude oil and still run a current-account deficit if it spends heavily on shipping, dividends to foreign oil companies and imported services. When a question says 'visible balance', it wants exports of goods minus imports of goods — nothing else.

points: Absolute advantage is higher productivity; comparative advantage is lower opportunity cost and is the basis of trade.
The balance of trade records visible goods; the balance of payments records all transactions, in a current account and a capital/financial account.
Protection uses tariffs, quotas, embargoes, exchange control and subsidies.
A BOP deficit can be tackled by devaluation, tighter demand policy, export promotion and attracting capital inflows.
In accounting terms the BOP balances; a 'deficit' means a shortfall being financed by borrowing or by reserve loss.
